input.body:
Follow-up to #1100 / #1105, now retargeted to `main`.

The technique #1105 used is worth writing down, and the skill that should carry it is the one about ordering a plan's phases: **a migration's cleanup is filed as work that comes back on its own, never written as a later phase.** A cleanup phase falls due long after the run that would have done it ended, and nothing brings it back; filed as a queued issue in the same change that creates the thing it cleans up, the owner can forget about it, which is the point.

It goes in the destructive-step exception in §1 — the paragraph that already names the migration's tail — plus a clause on finding 3 in the review list. Five lines net.

*(First draft was a 38-line section with its own heading. The owner's read on it — "very verbose for [one sentence]" — was right, and the section is gone.)*

### What changed, by folder

- **`packs/basics/skills/writing-migration-plans/`** — the rule, in §1's exception and finding 3.
- **`packs/basics/`** — the manifest version, since a pack's content is delivered on it.

# Verify in production

A change is finished when someone has watched it work. Most changes you can watch **now**, and
that is the rule — this skill is only for the rest: a change whose proof lives somewhere the
repo cannot see yet. It fires **automatically at the end of a change**, unasked. You are filing
the proof, not doing the work — and the proof itself runs unattended: an automatic check, end
to end, with a person entering only where no automatic check can exist.

## First: does this file anything at all?

Most changes **file nothing.** Run the test in this order and stop at the first answer:

1. **Did you watch it work in this session?** Then it is proven. File nothing.
2. **Did a test that ran prove it?** A unit test, a CI job, an executable-requirements or UI
   test covering exactly the behaviour that changed. File nothing — the suite is the mechanism
   that comes back.
3. **Does the change have an observable effect at all?** A comment, a design doc, a README, a
   rename with no behavioural edge, a refactor a passing suite already pins. File nothing.
4. **Otherwise: where does its effect first become observable?** If the answer is a place and a
   moment — a member repo once it converges, a site once it deploys, a session once it reloads
   its rules — that is what you file.

The bar is *could not be watched now*, not *would be nice to double-check*. A verification
filed for a change already covered by a test is a wasted run re-proving what the suite proved.

## What you file

**A deferred request** — the same ad-hoc lane `/do-later` rides, so the queue does the waiting,
the running and the lifecycle; nothing here adds machinery beside it. One issue, titled
`Verify in production: <the change, in a few words>`, its body the whole brief: the run that
verifies will never see this conversation and may be days away. Say what changed and why it
could not be watched now, then, each spelled verbatim on its own line:

```
Original-issue: #<the change's issue>
In-production-when: <the concrete artifact to read, and what makes it true>
Verify: <what to observe, and what counts as a pass>
Blocked-by: #<the change's PR>
Not-before: <ISO instant just past the expected release>
Retry-every: <how far to push Not-before when not yet live, e.g. 1 day>
```

- **`Original-issue:`** is where a failure lands — the issue the change was done under, which
  the run reopens if the verification fails. Make the verification that issue's **sub-issue**
  too (`mcp__github__sub_issue_write`, method `add`, `issue_number` the original,
  `sub_issue_id` the **id** the create call returned, not its number), so the change it proves
  shows what is still unproven about it.
- **`In-production-when:`** names a thing to *read*, never a duration to wait. "`missingbulb/Shepherd`'s
  `.claudinite-checks.json` stamps `packVersions.tidy-repo` at 8 or higher." "The live site's
  `/version.json` reports a version past 4.2.0." "Any session started after this landed — check
  the vendored copy under `.claudinite/shared/` carries the new text." A merge is not a
  production condition, and neither is elapsed time.
- **`Verify:`** is an assertion with a pass condition, not a topic — and a read an **unattended
  run can make**: an API response, a file at a URL, an issue's state. "Issue #100 on that repo
  is closed with a comment citing the scheduler runs" beats "check tidy-issues works". Only where no
  automatic check can exist may `Verify:` name a person's step, spelled out exactly.
- **`Blocked-by:`/`Not-before:`** are the queue's own wait fields: adoption holds the run until
  the PR has closed **and** the moment has passed. Aim `Not-before:` just past the release you
  expect — the re-arm covers a miss, so don't pad it.
- **`Retry-every:`** is the extension you are prescribing: when the run finds the change not
  yet live, it pushes `Not-before:` forward by exactly this much. Size it to the release you
  wait on — a nightly converge retries daily, a next-session rule in minutes.

Then the labels, as `/do-later` applies them: **`claude-task`** (the mark the scheduler run adopts) and
**`claude-model:sonnet`** (reading a live artifact and judging an assertion against it). Never
`claude-automerge` — a verification has nothing to merge. If `claude-task` doesn't exist in the
repo yet, say so and leave the issue — the labels appear on the next scheduler run.

## Tell the run how to converge

End the body with instructions to the run itself — the issue is its whole brief, and the run
decides nothing: it executes this playbook.

1. Read `In-production-when:` against the real artifact. Never infer it from a merge, a green
   run, or elapsed time.
2. **Live** → run `Verify:`. Passes: comment the evidence actually read (the version, the value,
   the URL) and close this issue as completed. Fails: reopen `Original-issue:` with a comment
   saying what was asserted, what happened instead and where you read it; comment here linking
   that; close this issue as completed — the verification did its job by finding the fault.
3. **Not yet live** → push `Not-before:` forward by `Retry-every:`, re-apply `claude-task` and
   `claude-model:sonnet`, and leave the issue open — the next scheduler run re-adopts it. No comment;
   the bumped field is the record.

## Then say what you filed

One line back to the owner: the issue link, what it waits on, and its retry cadence.

input.title: Verify in production: members re-stamp with date-anchored versions
input.body:
#1105 changed `ENGINE_VERSION` and every pack's `version` from a plain integer to a date-anchored string (`'60820.1'`), and widened every reader to take both. What that changes for a member is the shape of a value in **its own** `.claudinite-checks.json` — the stamp the update flows write and the fleet surfaces read.

It could not be watched in the session that landed it, for one reason: a member's stamp only moves when that member converges, which happens on its own nightly cycle. The canary rehearsal ([run 32371130795](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32371130795)) did prove the path end to end — a legacy-stamped member through both flows, mount self-test green — but on **one** repo, against the branch. What is unproven is the fleet: that every member's next converge re-stamps rather than parking, and that a member sitting mid-migration (new engine, packs not yet updated) is not left in a state its own vendored readers reject.

Original-issue: #1100
In-production-when: `missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary`'s `.claudinite-checks.json` on its default branch has `claudinite.engineVersion` matching `^\d{5,6}\.\d+$` rather than a bare integer.
Verify: read the same file on every member the fleet-roster tracker lists. Pass = every member's `claudinite.engineVersion` and every value in `claudinite.packVersions` is a date-anchored string, and no member has an open `needs-human` update PR whose reason mentions a version. Fail = any member still stamping a bare integer more than two of its own converge cycles after this landed, or any member parked with a version-shaped failure — name the member and quote the stamp.
Blocked-by: #1105
Not-before: 2026-08-22T06:00:00Z
Retry-every: 1 day

**For the run.**

1. Read `In-production-when:` against the real file over the API. Never infer it from this issue having merged, from a green Actions run, or from elapsed time.
2. **Live** → run `Verify:`. Passes: comment the stamps you actually read, member by member, and close this issue as completed. Fails: reopen #1100 with a comment saying what was asserted, what you found and where you read it; comment here linking that; close this issue as completed.
3. **Not yet live** → push `Not-before:` forward by one day, re-apply `claude-task` and `claude-model:sonnet`, leave this issue open. No comment — the bumped field is the record.

Note for a failing case: the tolerance in `engine/version.mjs` means a member holding a legacy integer is *behind*, never *broken*. A member still stamping integers is a converge that is not running, not a format that is not parsing — diagnose it as the former first.

content.text:
{"id":5203468097,"number":1100,"state":"closed","state_reason":"completed","locked":false,"title":"Engine and pack versions become date-anchored: `<ymmdd>.<n>`","body":"Engine and pack versions are monotonic integers today (`ENGINE_VERSION = 6`, `version: 13`). A number says nothing about *when* a version was cut, so "is this member behind, and by how long?" needs a second lookup every time.

Move both to a date-anchored form, `<ymmdd>.<n>` — `(year - 2020)*10000 + month*100 + day`, then a running number within that day. The first version cut on 2026-08-20 is `60820.1`, the second `60820.2`.

Ordering is unchanged in meaning: compare the day part, then the running number. Every legacy integer sorts below every date-anchored version (`6 < 60820.1`), so a member stamped under the old scheme reads as behind, which is what it is.

**Scope** — every site that creates, stamps, compares or scrapes a version:

- `engine/version.mjs` (`ENGINE_VERSION`), every `packs/*/pack.mjs` `version:`
- the comparators in `updates/{engine-update,pack-update,install}.mjs`
- `engine/checks/helpers/active-migrations.mjs` (record `version:` scrape, `migrationApplies`)
- `engine/pack_loader/pack-schema.mjs` (`isVersion`)
- the text scrapers in `packs/claudinite-dashboard/fleet.mjs` and `packs/claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/tasks/fleet-roster/drift-issues.mjs`
- the canon's own local checks `pack-version-bumped` and `engine-release-record`

**Migration technique**: every reader accepts both forms for one week; the legacy tolerance is removed in its own change once the fleet has re-stamped.

---

**Status**

- #1105 implements it. Engine release `60820.1`, qualified by canary rehearsal [run 32371130795](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32371130795) against `1f05d43`.
- #1106 is the queued removal of the legacy tolerance, blocked behind #1105, not to start before 2026-08-27.
- #1107 (stacked on #1105) writes the technique into the `writing-migration-plans` skill.

Two things the implementation settled that the brief did not:

- The year is anchored on **2020**, not taken as its last digit — `2026 → 6` either way, but a last-digit year wraps in 2030 and sorts a decade of releases underneath.
- A version is a **string**. `60820.10` and `60820.1` are different versions and the same float.

Legacy integers deliberately stay in two places until #1106: each pack's `minEngineVersion` floor and every migration record's `version:` range, both of which are references to engine versions that really were plain counters.

{"id":5203468097,"number":1100,"state":"closed","state_reason":"completed","locked":false,"title":"Engine and pack versions become date-anchored: `<ymmdd>.<n>`","body":"Engine and pack versions are monotonic integers today (`ENGINE_VERSION = 6`, `version: 13`). A number says nothing about *when* a version was cut, so "is this member behind, and by how long?" needs a second lookup every time.

Move both to a date-anchored form, `<ymmdd>.<n>` — `(year - 2020)*10000 + month*100 + day`, then a running number within that day. The first version cut on 2026-08-20 is `60820.1`, the second `60820.2`.

Ordering is unchanged in meaning: compare the day part, then the running number. Every legacy integer sorts below every date-anchored version (`6 < 60820.1`), so a member stamped under the old scheme reads as behind, which is what it is.

**Scope** — every site that creates, stamps, compares or scrapes a version:

- `engine/version.mjs` (`ENGINE_VERSION`), every `packs/*/pack.mjs` `version:`
- the comparators in `updates/{engine-update,pack-update,install}.mjs`
- `engine/checks/helpers/active-migrations.mjs` (record `version:` scrape, `migrationApplies`)
- `engine/pack_loader/pack-schema.mjs` (`isVersion`)
- the text scrapers in `packs/claudinite-dashboard/fleet.mjs` and `packs/claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/tasks/fleet-roster/drift-issues.mjs`
- the canon's own local checks `pack-version-bumped` and `engine-release-record`

**Migration technique**: every reader accepts both forms for one week; the legacy tolerance is removed in its own change once the fleet has re-stamped.

---

**Status**

- #1105 implements it. Engine release `60820.1`, qualified by canary rehearsal [run 32371130795](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32371130795) against `1f05d43`.
- #1106 is the queued removal of the legacy tolerance, blocked behind #1105, not to start before 2026-08-27.
- #1107 (stacked on #1105) writes the technique into the `writing-migration-plans` skill.

Two things the implementation settled that the brief did not:

- The year is anchored on **2020**, not taken as its last digit — `2026 → 6` either way, but a last-digit year wraps in 2030 and sorts a decade of releases underneath.
- A version is a **string**. `60820.10` and `60820.1` are different versions and the same float.

Legacy integers deliberately stay in two places until #1106: each pack's `minEngineVersion` floor and every migration record's `version:` range, both of which are references to engine versions that really were plain counters.

{"clone_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/shepherd","message":"Repo `missingbulb/shepherd` added. Clone it NOW — ONE clone, inline in this turn, not a subagent and not in parallel with anything else (the session's git proxy caps this repo at 2 concurrent smart-HTTP ops; a second clone 429s both). Run `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/missingbulb/shepherd /workspace/shepherd` — and give it a GENEROUS command timeout (≈10 min), not the default. A large repo's shallow pack can take 5–10 minutes through the proxy; the default ~2-min timeout will kill `git index-pack` mid-unpack and leave a broken half-clone. `index-pack` looks stalled while unpacking a big pack but isn't — do NOT interrupt, kill, or re-run it just because it's still going. 

If /workspace/shepherd already exists when you go to clone: do NOT `rm -rf` it reflexively — it may be a live clone (yours, or another turn's; this 'added' result is exactly what a second concurrent add sees). Check: `git -C /workspace/shepherd rev-parse HEAD` — if it succeeds, it's done, just use it. If it fails, watch `du -sh /workspace/shepherd/.git` across a few checks ~15s apart: if it's growing, a clone is live — wait. Only if rev-parse still fails AND `.git` has been the same size for ~60s is the clone dead. Even then, check `ls -A /workspace/shepherd` first: if it lists anything other than `.git`, the directory is NOT a dead half-clone — STOP, do not delete it, and tell the user the path is occupied. Only if it contains nothing but `.git`: `rm -rf /workspace/shepherd` then run the clone command above exactly once. 

If the clone fails with HTTP 429 / "Too many concurrent git operations", that is this session's local concurrency cap — NOT a GitHub rate limit. Sleep 10s (the Retry-After value) then retry exactly once. Do NOT retry in a loop and do NOT spawn more workers to try a different way. 

(Shallow; run `git -C /workspace/shepherd fetch --unshallow` later only if you need full history for blame/log/bisect.) After the clone succeeds, briefly report the outcome to the user and ask what they want to do with it. Do NOT say 'ready to clone' — the user already approved. Session currently has 2 repo(s): missingbulb/claudinite, missingbulb/shepherd.
